# Reverse Causality {.title-left}

<iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/oJgp-1esz00" title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## You'll learn to

::: presenter-space
- Define **reverse causality**.
- Identify relationships where causal direction is ambiguous.
- Explain why correlations alone cannot determine which way causation runs.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A familiar correlation

::: presenter-space
- Healthcare spending and CO₂ emissions are **positively correlated**.
- One interpretation: spending more on healthcare **causes** more emissions.
- In the previous video: national wealth may **confound** this relationship.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A second problem with the same correlation

::: presenter-space
- Confounding is not the only threat to causal interpretation.
- A second problem: we may have the **direction of causation backwards**.
- This is **reverse causality**.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Definition

::: presenter-space
**Reverse causality** occurs when:

- X and Y are correlated.
- We assume X causes Y.
- But Y may actually cause X — or causation runs **both ways**.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The reversed pathway: healthcare and emissions

::: presenter-space
- Higher emissions → more **pollution-related illness**.
- More illness → **greater demand** for healthcare.
- So emissions may drive spending, not the other way around.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Both directions may be plausible

::: presenter-space
- Wealthier, higher-emitting countries may also **invest more** in healthcare.
- But higher emissions may also **generate** healthcare need.
- The data alone cannot tell us which direction dominates.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example 1: Education and democracy

::: presenter-space
- More educated populations may **demand** democratic governance.
- But democracies may also **invest more** in public education.
- Does education cause democracy, or democracy cause education?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example 2: Policing and crime

::: presenter-space
- More police may **deter** criminal activity.
- But higher crime rates may **prompt** increases in policing.
- The observed correlation is consistent with **both** directions.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The core difficulty

::: presenter-space
- Observational data show that X and Y move **together**.
- They cannot tell us whether X drives Y, Y drives X, or **both**.
- Establishing causal direction requires more than a correlation.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Recap

::: presenter-space
- Reverse causality: Y may cause X, not just X causing Y.
- The healthcare–emissions correlation is consistent with **both** directions.
- Correlations alone cannot resolve which direction causation runs.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: presenter-space
**Why this matters:**

- Causal claims based on correlations appear constantly in public debate.
- Reverse causality is one reason those claims may be wrong.
- Recognising it is crucial for evaluating quantitative evidence critically.
:::
